title: PROMPT: PRObabilistic Memory Trees for Efficient Skill Reuse in Robotics
abstract: Modern simulation platforms support massively parallel rollouts, precise environment modeling, and flexible task design, making them well-suited for large-scale acquisition of manipulation skills. Yet current skill learning algorithms remain sample-inefficient, often depending on massive initialization and replay, particularly when learning complex manipulation skills across diverse environments. To resolve these challenges, we present PROMPT, a retrieval-augmented lifelong learning framework that enables efficient reuse of prior knowledge and rapid adaptation to novel tasks and environments. During each run, PROMPT constructs and maintains a hierarchical probabilistic skill tree that stores previously acquired skills together with the semantic, geometric, and spatial information of their associated tasks and environments. When a new task arrives, PROMPT performs probabilistic localization to retrieve similar skills from the tree for model initialization and integrates the newly learned skill into the tree in an online fashion. Our empirical study shows that PROMPT achieves significant sample efficiency improvements and accuracy across diverse environments and manipulation tasks compared to learning from scratch. Notably, in Pick & Place tasks, it reaches a 1.0 success rate with 20% fewer steps, while in Open/Close tasks, it reduces the running steps by 25% and simultaneously improves average success.

title: CARoL: Context-Aware Adaptation for Robot Learning
abstract: Using Reinforcement Learning (RL) to learn new robotic tasks from scratch is often inefficient. Leveraging prior knowledge has the potential to significantly enhance learning efficiency, which, however, raises two critical challenges: how to determine the relevancy of existing knowledge and how to adaptively integrate them into learning a new task variants with differing dynamics. In this paper, we propose Context-aware Adaptation for Robot Learning (CARoL), a novel framework to efficiently learn a similar but distinct new task from prior knowledge. CARoL incorporates context awareness by analyzing state transitions in system dynamics to identify similarities between the new task and prior knowledge. It then utilizes these identified similarities to prioritize and adapt specific knowledge pieces for the new task. Additionally, CARoL has a broad applicability spanning policy-based, value-based, and actor-critic RL algorithms. We validate the efficiency and generalizability of CARoL on both simulated robotic platforms and physical ground vehicles. Simulations include CarRacing and LunarLander environments, where CARoL demonstrates faster convergence and higher rewards when learning policies for new tasks. In real-world experiments, we show that CARoL enables a ground vehicle to quickly and efficiently adapt policies learned in simulation to smoothly traverse real-world off-road terrain.

title: MyoDEA: A Self-Sensing Dielectric Elastomer Actuator for Real-Time Muscle Stiffness Monitoring
abstract: Monitoring muscle stiffness in real-time during dynamic muscle activity is critical for rehabilitation, athletic training, and human-robot interaction. Existing technologies often require bulky hardware and complex multi-component systems, limiting reliable stiffness measurement in daily activities. In this work, we introduce MyoDEA, a centimeter scale and 770mg device based on a novel self-sensing dielectric elastomer actuator (DEA) for time-varying muscle stiffness detection. This DEA generates a 2.5 times higher blocked force than previously reported power-dense DEAs at operating frequencies below 10Hz, while maintaining comparable bandwidth and energy output at resonance. A new self-sensing method is also developed to enable integrated actuation and sensing within a single DEA. The MyoDEA achieves continuous muscle stiffness tracking at 10Hz over a range of 30kPa to 140kPa. Human-subject experiments with MyoDEA worn on the forearm over the flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) muscle belly demonstrate reliable continuous stiffness tracking during isometric gripping across 0%–80% maximum voluntary contraction (%MVC).

title: BiFlex: A Passive Bimodal Stiffness Flexible Wrist for Manipulation in Unstructured Environments
abstract: Robotic manipulation in unstructured, human-centric environments poses a dual challenge: achieving the precision needed for delicate free-space operation while ensuring safety during unexpected contact events. Traditional wrists struggle to balance these demands, often relying on complex control schemes or complicated mechanical designs to mitigate potential damage from force overload. In response, we present BiFlex, a flexible robotic wrist that uses a soft buckling honeycomb structure to provide a natural bimodal stiffness response. The higher stiffness mode enables precise household object manipulation, while the lower stiffness mode provides the compliance needed to adapt to external forces. We design BiFlex to maintain a fingertip deflection of less than 1 cm while supporting loads up to 500g and create a BiFlex wrist for many grippers, including Panda, Robotiq, and BaRiFlex. We validate BiFlex under several real-world experimental evaluations, including surface wiping, precise pick-and-place, and grasping under environmental constraints. We demonstrate that BiFlex simplifies control while maintaining precise object manipulation and enhanced safety in real-world applications. More information and videos at https://robin-lab.cs.utexas.edu/BiFlex/

title: Designing Autonomous Behavioral Switching in Eight-Armed Octopus-Like Soft Robot: Physical Reservoir Computing Approach
abstract: Biological behavior emerges as a consequence of interactions among the brain, the body, and the environment, and physical reservoir computing has been proposed as one of the frameworks for exploiting such dynamical couplings as a computational resource in robotics. In this study, we developed an octopus-like robot featuring eight arms each equipped with sensors, four passive and four active. Systematic analyses of the body dynamics show that the passive arms receive inputs from the active arms through the body and the environment, thereby drastically modulating the memory profile of the entire body as a reservoir. This enhanced capability enables the robot to exhibit both untrained behavior with the external physical input and switch among trained behaviors via a control signal using a single output layer. Furthermore, from the perspective of multifunctional reservoir computing, this study provides the first example demonstrating a physical robot autonomously switching among predesigned behaviors triggered by changes in environmental conditions. These results further expand the prospects for embodied intelligence.

title: Octopus-Inspired Distributed Control for Soft Robotic Arms: A Graph Neural Network–Based Attention Policy with Environmental Interaction
abstract: This paper proposes SoftGM, an octopus-inspired distributed control architecture for segmented soft robotic arms that learn to reach targets in contact-rich environments using online obstacle discovery without relying on global obstacle geometry. SoftGM formulates each arm section as a cooperative agent and represents the arm-environment interaction as a graph. SoftGM uses a two-stage graph attention message passing scheme following a Centralised Training Decentralised Execution (CTDE) paradigm with a centralised critic and decentralised actor. We evaluate SoftGM in a Cosserat-rod simulator (PyElastica) across three tasks that increase the complexity of the environment: obstacle-free, structured obstacles, and a wall-with-hole scenario. Compared with six widely used MARL baselines (IDDPG, IPPO, ISAC, MADDPG, MAPPO, MASAC) under identical information content and training conditions, SoftGM matches strong CTDE methods in simpler settings and achieves the best performance in the wall-with-hole task. Robustness tests with observation noise, single-section actuation failure, and transient disturbances show that SoftGM preserves success while keeping control effort bounded, indicating resilient coordination driven by selective contact-relevant information routing.

title: Robot-To-Robot Tactile Communication in Resource-Limited, Small-Scale Robots
abstract: Mechanical communication in insects motivates alternative messaging modalities for robots operating under limited resources or in disconnected, intermittent, low-bandwidth (DIL) environments. We introduce a tactile communication framework for mobile robots in which binary messages are transmitted via physical contact and decoded as digital input transitions. Each robot integrates a flexible antenna structure that functions as a binary switch. Building on this hardware, we develop a UART-inspired protocol. We demonstrate the system on 7.2 g differential-drive robots with onboard power and computation, and quantify communication performance across 120 robot-to-robot trials spanning four 2-bit messages. To evaluate scaling behavior, we embed experimentally derived contact and decoding probabilities into an agent-based swarm model and analyze message propagation under the gossip or susceptible–infected models, revealing population and density-dependent trade-offs between propagation speed and full convergence. This work positions tactile contact as a communication paradigm for resource-constrained robot systems.

title: HJCD-IK: GPU-Accelerated Inverse Kinematics through Batched Hybrid Jacobian Coordinate Descent
abstract: Inverse Kinematics (IK) is a core problem in robotics, in which joint configurations are found to achieve a (collision-free) desired end-effector pose. Modern IK solvers face a fundamental trade-off: analytical methods are fast but lack generality, while numerical optimization-based methods are broadly applicable but prone to local minima and high computational costs. To overcome this challenge, we introduce HJCD-IK, a GPU-accelerated, sampling-based hybrid solver. By pairing a novel orientation-aware greedy coordinate descent initialization with Jacobian-based polishing and a parallel collision filter, our method achieves up to order-of-magnitude gains in speed and accuracy over state-of-the-art solvers, consistently finding collision-free solutions on the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier, while producing a diverse distribution of high-quality samples. We validate our solver on a physical Franka manipulator and release our code open-source.

title: Dense-Joint-Based Obstacle-Aided Locomotion with a Joint-Repositionable Snake Robot
abstract: Obstacle-aided locomotion is a fundamental capability for snake robots to traverse complex environments. However, conventional rigid-link snake robots often suffer from stagnation or jamming due to low joint density (i.e., the number of joints per unit length), which causes discontinuous contact with obstacles, unlike the continuous adaptation of biological snakes. To investigate the effect of joint density on obstacle-aided locomotion performance, we utilized a joint-repositionable snake robot mechanism that decouples actuators from joints, enabling a high-density architecture. We developed two experimental models with identical total lengths but different joint densities (high-density and low-density) and conducted comparative propulsion experiments in peg-based obstacle environments with varying peg diameters. The experimental results demonstrate that the high-density model significantly suppresses the abrupt shifts in reaction forces that cause stagnation in the low-density model. By maintaining smooth contact points, the high-density configuration reduces power consumption and achieves stable, continuous propulsion. These results highlight high joint density as a key factor in improving the environmental adaptability of snake robots in complex terrains.

title: A Simple Three-Link Passive Suspension Mechanism for Enhancing Ground Contact and Stability in Omnidirectional Mobile Robots
abstract: This paper introduces a simple yet novel three-link passive suspension mechanism designed to enhance ground contact and stability in omnidirectional mobile robots. The proposed system ensures consistent wheel ground contact, which is critical for achieving stable acceleration, deceleration, and maneuverability. This study focuses on the concept of "acceleration threshold," defined as the critical acceleration immediately prior to wheel lift-off. Through comprehensive analysis, both longitudinal and lateral acceleration thresholds are evaluated, with a particular emphasis on lateral acceleration threshold. Additionally, the study explores the impact of the robot's center of mass position along the longitudinal axis on lateral acceleration threshold, demonstrating that optimal design choices can enhance overall safety. This research provides valuable insights for optimizing ground contact and stability in omnidirectional robots.

title: Multi-Degree-Of-Freedom Planar Linkage Synthesis for Leg Designs
abstract: Linkage synthesis methods help design and tune robot legs for specific applications. This paper proposes a topological and dimensional linkage synthesis tool for multi-degree-of-freedom (DoF) planar linkages with revolute joints. It enumerates a large number of topologies with analytical forward kinematics and synthesizes their dimensions with gradient-based optimization. The optimization not only supports a variety of costs and constraints for specifying design requirements, but is also fast and scalable with parallel computation on graphics processing units. Three leg examples, including a one-DoF leg for walking mechanisms, a two-DoF parallel leg with a fan-shaped workspace, and a three-DoF hybrid leg with an active ankle, are designed and validated in the real world. This tool also has potential for grippers, wings, arms and more.

title: A Wheel-Gripper: Enabling Multifunctionality through Factorability
abstract: Manipulation with legs on multi-pedal robots is not a new concept, but it has rarely been considered on wheel-legged robots due to their mechanical structure. This paper presents a mechanism that transitions between a wheel and a gripper, allowing wheel-legged robots to perform manipulation tasks with their legs. It is capable of storing small objects, liquid, or soil while still functioning as a wheel. The design utilizes two distinctive kinematic modes for these functionalities, and uses only one motor for both wheeled locomotion and gripping, with no new actuator for transitioning or locking. Our analysis showed that those distinctive modes corresponded to the factors of the complex kinematics polynomials of the mechanism. The two modes exist because the polynomials that govern the mechanism's kinematics factor. That is to say, its overall motion is the union of two lower degree irreducible components. A single-leg platform was built to demonstrate its ability to grasp objects and collect water or soil samples, and explore its capability as a contact force sensor through experiments. Such a design could enable wheel-legged robots to perform more diverse loco-manipulation tasks without installing additional limbs.

title: Design and Control of D6SR: A Mechanically Decoupled Six-Axis Spherical Rolling Robot for Stable Propeller-Driven Rolling
abstract: Propeller-driven spherical robots can generate strong rolling actuation. However, most existing designs rigidly connect the propulsion module to the outer shell. As the shell rotates, the thrust direction also changes continuously in the inertial frame. Maintaining a desired propulsion direction therefore often requires frequent reversals of the motors. This paper presents D6SR, a mechanically decoupled six-axis spherical rolling robot. It uses a three-degree-of-freedom gimbal mechanism to separate shell rotation from the orientation of the internal propulsion module. As a result, the outer shell can roll while the internal body remains stabilized. The thrust direction can therefore remain consistent during motion. We first develop a cascaded PID stabilizer for basic attitude control. We then train a residual reinforcement-learning policy on top of this controller. The policy is trained in simulation using inertial-navigation measurements. The results show that residual RL improves rolling stability and robustness on complex terrain. Both simulation and real-robot experiments are conducted. The robot maintains a consistent thrust direction and achieves stable rolling. These results validate the proposed mechanical decoupling mechanism and control strategy for a six-axis spherical rolling robot.

title: Design and Control of a Novel Hybrid Typed Outdoor Mobile Robot Platform: MobED
abstract: Mobile robot platforms are increasingly utilized in various automation applications due to advancements in platforms and autonomous navigation. Outdoor mobility places tougher requirements on robot platforms than indoor environments, and is thus being actively researched. In this paper, we propose a novel mobile robot platform with a unique mechanical design and control methodology developed to address the limitations of previous mobile robots. The robot, with 12 active degrees of freedom (DoFs), is devised to combine the ground-adaptability of legged platforms with the advantages of a wheeled platform such as high payload and energy efficiency. Its independent steering/driving system enables mobility beyond car-like driving, and the posture control system based on an eccentric mechanism allows body roll/pitch control and body height adjustment, which enable stable driving and carrying payloads. A modular control architecture was developed to provide a holonomic driving mode with ground adaptation. In this architecture, the driving control was implemented based on kinematics and the balance control was implemented by combined position/force control adjusted via a gain scheduling technique.We verified that the robot achieved stable driving on irregular terrain despite disturbed roll-pitch body posture and was capable of carrying a payload up to 56 kg indoors and outdoors.

title: An Orthogonal-Axis Spherical Parallel Mechanism with Large Workspace for Humanoid Hip Joints: Design, Optimization, and Experimental Validation
abstract: Conventional serial-chain configurations for humanoid robot lower limbs exhibit issues such as concentrated driving torques, inertial coupling, and error accumulation, leading to inadequate joint stiffness, limited control precision, and reduced dynamic stability. To overcome these drawbacks, this study proposes a novel Orthogonal-axis Spherical Parallel Mechanism, inspired by the ball-and-socket structure of the human hip joint. The kinematic model of the mechanism is established. A multi-objective optimization framework is then constructed, considering workspace coverage, dexterity, and maximum joint torque, and optimal parameters are obtained through weighted decision-making. Simulations and experiments verify that the optimized mechanism fully covers the common range of motion of the human hip joint, demonstrates improved dexterity within common motion ranges, and supports a single-leg payload of 40 kg. Integrating high stiffness, a large workspace, and superior load capability, this design offers a comprehensive solution for humanoid robotic legs.

title: CHUTNI: Compensated Holonomic Uneven Terrain Isolator
abstract: We present CHUTNI (Compensated Holonomic Uneven Terrain Isolator), an off-road differential-drive with offset turret platform that delivers holonomic control of a stabilized turret on uneven terrain. CHUTNI uses simple drive wheels on a rocker suspension to keep both wheels in contact with the ground, while an actively stabilized gimbal with three degrees of freedom, i.e., roll, pitch, and yaw, holds the turret at a commanded pose with respect to the world frame. The result is lateral, longitudinal, yaw, roll, and pitch motions that can be commanded independently at the turret, with the robot chassis free to absorb the terrain irregularities. We evaluate the physical CHUTNI and also in simulation on test courses and quantify its holonomicity using the mobility ellipsoid. Experiments demonstrate holonomic turret motion and arbitrary trajectory execution without stop-to-reorient behavior as seen in robots with non-holonomic bases.

title: Fast-BEV++: Fast by Algorithm, Deployable by Design
abstract: The advancement of vision-only BEV (Bird’s-Eye-View) perception is hindered by the fundamental trade-off between perception accuracy and deployment efficiency. We introduce Fast-BEV++, resolving this tension through two principles: Fast by Algorithm and Deployable by Design. By decomposing view transformation into a hardware-oriented Index-Gather-Reshape pipeline, Fast-BEV++ eliminates custom kernels while achieving no less than 3× speedup over baseline methods. Empirically, Fast-BEV++ establishes a new state-of-the-art accuracy-speed trade-off on nuScenes, achieving 0.488 NDS while sustaining real-time inference at over 134 FPS. In particular, depth supervision yields consistent and tangible performance gains, maintaining the highest accuracy among comparable methods. The decomposed architecture enables seamless real-time deployment on production-level platforms, eliminating hardware constraints without loss of efficiency.

title: DPNeXt: A Lightweight Multi-Scale Feature Fusion Framework for Efficient ViT-Based Multi-Task Dense Prediction
abstract: Multi-Task Learning (MTL) in robotics perception systems supports comprehensive 3D spatial scene understanding by integrating semantic segmentation and depth estimation. While Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) are increasingly adopted as robust feature encoders, existing decoding strategies present a critical bottleneck. To address this, we propose DPNeXt, a streamlined multi-scale feature fusion decoder and efficient alternative to the standard Dense Prediction Transformer (DPT). DPNeXt uses dual depthwise separable inverted bottlenecks to improve frozen VFM utilization through fusion-centric decoding and independent task modularization. To further mitigate negative inductive transfer between tasks, we introduce the Multi-Task Boundary Guidance (MTBG) strategy. Unlike prior boundary-aware methods that add fusion modules or gating, MTBG applies symmetric boundary-focused supervision to encourage geometric consistency without extra annotation or inference cost. Experiments on Cityscapes show that DPNeXt-S outperforms prior state-of-the-art (SOTA) MTL models, while DPNeXt-B further improves the overall performance and achieves the best results among the compared methods. On NYUv2, DPNeXt-B also achieves the best semantic segmentation and depth estimation results among the compared methods while requiring substantially fewer trainable parameters than prior large-scale MTL models. Compared with the standard DPT, DPNeXt-S reduces trainable parameters by 78.4% and achieves the fastest inference speed among the compared models on resource-constrained laptop hardware. The source code, model checkpoints, and a demo video will be made available at https://github.com/kangjehun/DPNeXt.

title: DGSA: Bridging Spectral Frequencies with Cross-Attention for Point Cloud Adaptation
abstract: Point cloud learning is fundamental to robotic perception, enabling tasks such as autonomous driving, object manipulation, and scene understanding. Full fine-tuning of large point cloud backbones is computationally prohibitive, yet existing parameter-efficient methods fail to capture both global topology and local geometric detail simultaneously. We present DGSA (Dual-stream Graph Spectral Adapter), a PEFT framework that processes global structure via Graph Fourier Transform and local multi-scale features via Chebyshev polynomial wavelets within a unified spectral representation. The two streams are fused coherently in the spectral domain, enabling global structural priors to guide local feature refinement. To bridge these complementary frequency bands, DGSA introduces Spectral Cross-Attention (O(N) complexity) for bidirectional low-to-high frequency interaction, and BandMamba for linear-time long-range dependency modeling across the full spectral sequence. With only 1.6M trainable parameters (0.44% of the backbone), DGSA achieves state-of-the-art results without voting: 99.31% on ScanObjectNN OBJ-BG, 86.94% instance mIoU on ShapeNetPart—surpassing full fine-tuning—and 98.1% on ModelNet40 10-way 20-shot few-shot classification.

title: SemanticFlow: A Self-Supervised Framework for Joint Scene Flow Prediction and Instance Segmentation in Dynamic Environments
abstract: Accurate perception of dynamic traffic scenes is crucial for high-level autonomous driving systems, requiring robust object motion estimation and instance segmentation. However, traditional methods often treat these tasks independently, leading to suboptimal performance, spatio-temporal inconsistencies, and limited information sharing in complex dynamic scenarios. This paper proposes a multi-task SemanticFlow framework to jointly predict scene flow and instance segmentation on full-resolution point clouds. The novelty of this work are threefold: 1) developing a two-stage refinement based multi-task scheme, where an initial coarse segmentation of static backgrounds and dynamic objects provides contextual priors for refining motion and semantic representations through a shared feature processing module; 2) designing a set of mutually-constraining loss functions to enhance both scene flow estimation and instance segmentation, while promoting spatial and temporal consistency of static and dynamic objects in traffic scenes; 3) introducing a self-supervised learning strategy, which leverages coarse segmentation to identify rigid objects and estimate their transformation matrices between sequential frames, enabling the generation of reliable supervisory signals without manual annotations. The proposed framework is evaluated on the Argoverse and Waymo datasets, demonstrating competitive results and consistent improvements over existing self-supervised approaches for dynamic scene understanding. The source code and trained model weights will be publicly released upon publication to facilitate reproducibility.

title: StreamDiffMap: Efficient Vectorized Online HD Map Construction Via Streaming Truncated Diffusion
abstract: Online vectorized HD map construction is pivotal for autonomous driving systems to comprehend complex road topologies. While diffusion models excel at generating consistent and long-range map structures, their reliance on iterative denoising from pure Gaussian noise imposes prohibitive inference latency and optimization challenges, hindering real-time deployment. To bridge this gap, we propose StreamDiffMap, an efficient framework based on streaming truncated diffusion. Rather than merely accelerating the sampling schedule, our core insight centers on reducing the inherent denoising difficulty by leveraging the rich temporal correlation in video streams. Specifically, we utilize motion-compensated historical predictions as dynamic anchors, shifting the perception paradigm from global generation-from-scratch to efficient local geometric refinement. To realize this paradigm, we introduce a Content-Geometry Decoupled Query (CGDQ) to explicitly encapsulate dynamic geometric priors, alongside a Training-Inference Consistent Warm-up (TIC-Warmup) strategy to mitigate distribution shift and error accumulation during streaming. Extensive experiments on the nuScenes dataset demonstrate that StreamDiffMap achieves 65.1% mAP, outperforming the generative baseline by a substantial 14.9% margin. Remarkably, by requiring only a single denoising step, our method delivers a 23% inference speedup (12.4 FPS on RTX 4090D), proving that generative models can deliver competitive map construction capabilities with significantly reduced latency.

title: Towards Practical Scene Change Detection: A Fast, Unaligned Video Framework Via Spatiotemporal Alignment
abstract: Scene change detection (SCD) is crucial for long-term robot autonomy but faces significant hurdles: the lack of temporal alignment in real-world video streams and the high latency of existing foundation model-based methods. To bridge the gap towards practical deployment, we propose a unified framework for unaligned videos captured during repeated traversals. First, we introduce a robust temporal alignment strategy integrating visual place recognition (VPR) with FastDTW, enabling reliable frame pairing even in visually degraded environments where standard retrieval fails. Second, we present FastGeSCF, a highly generalizable architecture that accelerates inference by replacing dense prompting with a novel coarse-to-fine selective prompting mechanism. By leveraging a cross-attention pseudo-mask generator and a grid point filter, we selectively prompt the Segment Anything Model (SAM) only at relevant regions. Experiments demonstrate that our method maintains competitive accuracy compared to computationally expensive baselines while reducing inference time by approximately 7.9 times (~0.88 s/pair). This efficiency-accuracy balance makes it a viable solution for online robotic applications.

title: Object-Centric State-Guided SAM for Temporally Coherent Multi-Object Segmentation in Complex Underwater Environments
abstract: Robust perception in complex underwater environments is critical for marine resource exploration, ecological monitoring, and robotic operations, yet remains challenging due to low visibility, color distortion, dynamic backgrounds, and long-term occlusions. Although foundation models such as SAM 2 demonstrate strong segmentation performance on static imagery, their lack of explicit temporal modeling limits reliability in underwater video scenarios. To address this limitation, we propose AquaSlot-SAM, a hybrid object-centric temporal segmentation framework that integrates Slot-based State Space Models (SlotSSMs) with prompt-guided refinement in SAM 2. SlotSSMs explicitly maintain object-level temporal states, which are converted into adaptive prompts to guide SAM 2 toward spatially precise and temporally coherent segmentation. A sparse Slot Mixer enhances inter-object interaction, while confidence-aware mask fusion balances global stability and local boundary refinement. Extensive experiments on three public underwater benchmarks demonstrate that AquaSlot-SAM consistently outperforms strong contemporary baselines, achieving substantial improvements across multiple metrics and validating the effectiveness of structured memory-guided prompting for dynamic underwater segmentation.

title: Force Feedback for Robust Excavator Teleoperation under Visual Uncertainty
abstract: Teleoperating heavy machinery improves safety by separating operators from hazardous sites, yet performance often deteriorates when operators rely on delayed or degraded video feedback. This study investigates whether kinesthetic force feedback can enhance control robustness under degraded visual conditions in excavator teleoperation. A high-fidelity simulator was developed with configurable video delay and resolution to reproduce controlled forms of visual degradation, enabling systematic analysis of the interaction between visual and force-feedback channels. Four trained operators performed a rock dig-and-dump task under eight combinations of force feedback and video conditions. Force feedback improved efficiency, productivity, and force modulation. Across the tested visual conditions, task completion time decreased by up to 20%, trajectory length by up to 19%, failure rate by up to 56%, and mean contact force by up to 22%. Operators completed tasks faster, followed shorter bucket-tip trajectories, and applied lower average contact forces without a systematic increase in peak contact force. The persistence of these benefits under degraded visual conditions suggests that force feedback can help compensate for uncertainty caused by video delay and reduced resolution. These results support the use of kinesthetic force feedback as a complementary sensory channel for robust excavator teleoperation under visual uncertainty, providing a practical foundation for future human-in-the-loop operation of heavy machinery.

title: Sensorless Four-Channel Control Architecture Using Inverse Dynamics Modeling for Human-Scale Bilateral Teleoperation
abstract: The four-channel teleoperation architecture is a well-established framework for achieving transparency in bilateral systems. However, its performance in human-scale teleoperation is limited by high inertia, modeling challenges, and reliance on noisy and costly force/torque sensors. This paper introduces a sensorless four-channel architecture based on inverse dynamics modeling. The controller is implemented and validated on a customized WAM bilateral teleoperation setup. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms conventional two- and four-channel schemes as well as transparency-enhancement methods, improving position and force tracking, reducing operator effort, and increasing maximum transmittable impedance without external sensors. A door-opening case study involving sustained whole-body contact along the manipulator further demonstrates the effectiveness of the method in realistic human-scale manipulation tasks.

title: Exploiting Passive Low-Level Control Dissipating Capabilities to Leverage TDPA Passivity Layer in Teleoperation
abstract: Ensuring stability in bilateral teleoperation remains a significant challenge due to the destabilizing effects of communication delays. While the Time Domain Passivity Approach (TDPA) restores stability, its inherent overconservatism often leads to excessive energy dissipation, degrading force transparency and motion synchronization. Recent advancements, such as Energy-Reflection TDPA, mitigate this issue by modeling the communication channel as a virtual spring; however, these methods are often architecture-dependent and fail to fully exploit the dissipative potential of local controllers. This paper proposes a conceptually different framework: the extended Time Delay Power Network. By shifting the network boundaries to internalize the Low-Level Control, the eTDPN exploits the inherent physical damping of local controllers to absorb part of the energy introduced by an active behaviour of the communication channel. Theoretically, the eTDPN is proven to be superior to traditional TDPN implementations by construction, as the energy demand at the Passivity Controller is systematically reduced. Furthermore, the proposed strategy is side-agnostic and architecture-independent, facilitating a straightforward implementation for multi-DoFs systems without requiring inter-controller data exchange. The framework was validated through a user study involving 10 participants using a Position-Force computed architecture with a 200 ms round-trip delay. Statistical results demonstrate that eTDPN significantly outperforms TDPA-ER by reducing both the dissipation demand and the actual energy removed by the PCs, thereby enhancing haptic fidelity while maintaining guaranteed global stability.

title: TASC: Task-Aware Shared Control for Relational Telemanipulation
abstract: We present TASC, a Task-Aware Shared Control framework for relational telemanipulation that infers task-level user intent and provides assistance from motion-only input. To support prehensile relational tasks without predefined templates, TASC constructs an open-vocabulary interaction graph from visual input to represent functional object relationships, and infers user intent accordingly. A shared control policy then provides assistance during both grasping and object interaction, guided by spatial constraints predicted by a vision-language model. Our method addresses two key challenges in relational telemanipulation under shared control: (1) task-level intent inference from low-level motion commands, and (2) generalizable assistance across diverse objects and tasks. Experiments in both simulation and the real world demonstrate that TASC improves task efficiency and reduces user input effort compared to prior methods, while enabling zero-shot generalization across diverse relational telemanipulation tasks. The code that supports our experiments is publicly available at https://github.com/fitz0401/tasc.

title: TRIP-Bag: A Portable Teleoperation System for Plug-And-Play Robotic Arms and Leaders
abstract: Large scale, diverse demonstration data for manipulation tasks remains a major challenge in learning-based robot policies. Existing in-the-wild data collection approaches often rely on vision-based pose estimation of hand-held grippers or gloves, which introduces an embodiment gap between the collection platform and the target robot. Teleoperation systems eliminate the embodiment gap, but are typically impractical to deploy outside the laboratory environment. We propose TRIP-Bag (Teleoperation, Recording, Intelligence in a Portable Bag), a portable, puppeteer-style teleoperation system fully contained within a commercial suitcase, as a practical solution for collecting high-fidelity manipulation data across varied settings. With a setup time of under five minutes and direct joint-to-joint teleoperation, TRIP-Bag enables rapid and reliable data collection in any environment. We validated TRIP-Bag’s usability through experiments with non-expert users, showing that the system is intuitive and easy to operate. Furthermore, we confirmed the quality of the collected data by training benchmark manipulation policies, demonstrating its value as a practical resource for robot learning.

title: LoGo: A Low-Cost, General-Purpose Teleoperation Framework for Mobile Manipulation
abstract: High-quality demonstration data remains scarce for mobile manipulation, where robots must coordinate dexterous arm control with agile base navigation, yet existing teleoperation systems are often costly, hardware-specific, or decouple locomotion from manipulation. We present LoGo, a sub-$400 handheld framework that unifies bimanual manipulation and whole-body mobile control by integrating 3D-printed master arms with consumer Joy-Cons. A dual-mode kinematic framework supports both isomorphic joint mapping and Cartesian IK retargeting, enabling concurrent control of mobile bases, lifts, and dexterous end-effectors. By combining passive gravity-compensated master arms with IMU-augmented Joy-Cons, LoGo offers a compact, handheld form factor that does not require external tracking infrastructure. Its modular software stack allows rapid deployment across fixed-base, mobile, and simulated robots without hardware reconfiguration. Experiments in simulation and the real world show LoGo achieves a 0.94 success rate and 8.9/10 user rating, significantly outperforming keyboard, VR controller, and ACE baselines. Imitation learning policies trained on LoGo-collected data exceed 80% success on long-horizon precision tasks, confirming its ability to produce high-fidelity data for robot learning. These characteristics make LoGo a practical and scalable solution for collecting diverse demonstrations that advance imitation learning and VLA models in mobile manipulation.

title: Investigating the Effects of Form Factor on Mobile Device-Based Robot Teleoperation for Dexterous Tasks
abstract: Robot teleoperation remains an important subfield of robotics, enabling human operators to execute tasks in hazardous or otherwise inaccessible environments. Despite its effectiveness, traditional teleoperation often relies on specialized, high-cost hardware, which limits broader accessibility and large-scale deployment. Recently, the ubiquity and extensive use of mobile devices, frequently equipped with geospatial sensors and cameras, have offered a low-cost alternative for mapping human motion to robotic states. However, the influence of the physical device form factor on operator performance remains under-explored in telerobotic contexts. Consequently, we investigated how differences in form factor, specifically between a smartphone and a tablet, affect teleoperation efficiency. We performed a within-subject user study (n=16) to systematically evaluate performance metrics and subjective experience. Our results indicate that the device form factor has a statistically significant impact on completion time (p = 0.012) and error rates (p = 0.028), as well as on perceived usability (p = 0.041) and usefulness (p = 0.035), revealing better task outcomes for the larger device (tablet) while subjective preference between devices remained inconclusive. Using a larger tablet form factor as a control device can reduce average operation times and total number of errors by ≈ 33% and ≈ 53%, respectively, while simultaneously increasing control stability, and enabling more effective dexterous task execution. These results offer key insights for the design of future mobile device-based robotic teleoperation interfaces.

title: An Adaptive Finite-Time Convergent Neural Network with Enhanced Joint Limit Constraints for 3-DoF Visual Servoing of Rigid-Flexible Coupling Robots
abstract: Recently, researchers have employed visual servoing to automate rigid-flexible coupling robots and develop a quadratic programming (QP) framework to manage their behavior, thereby demonstrating great potential in industry and other fields. However, fast real-time solutions for such redundant systems remain challenging. Therefore, we propose a novel adaptive finite-time convergent neural network (AFTCNN) to address time-varying redundancy problems with joint limit constraints, which is successfully applied to visual servoing of automated rigid-flexible coupling robots (VSARFCR). First, a QP-based 3-DoF visual tracking control scheme that considers tracking error, joint limit constraints, and joint-drifting issues is constructed based on the VSARFCR kinematics model. A new enhanced joint limit handling technology is specifically designed for VSARFCR with a prismatic joint. Then, a novel AFTCNN is proposed to address the aforementioned QP-based control scheme with various objectives and constraints. Next, the finite-time convergence of the proposed AFTCNN is rigorously proven using Lyapunov theory. Finally, simulations and physical experiments demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed control scheme for 3-DoF visual tracking under diverse constraints and objectives. Compared with existing methods, the proposed AFTCNN exhibits faster convergence and improved solution accuracy for redundancy resolution in VSARFCR.

title: GAASP: Graph-Based Automated Assembly Sequencing and Planning
abstract: Assembly planning, determining feasible sequences and collision-free paths to construct products from individual parts, is essential for modern manufacturing, yet remains computationally challenging due to combinatorial search spaces and narrow passage constraints. We present a contact graph-guided assembly planning algorithm that achieves unprecedented scalability by exploiting graph topology as a geometric accessibility metric. Our key insight: parts with higher accessibility have fewer contacts with neighboring components, and hence they appear in the contact graph as vertices with a lower degree. We introduce an assembly-aware depth-first search that systematically traverses the contact graph from high-degree (interior) to low-degree (exterior) vertices, and is tightly integrated with a physics solver using discrete force directions. We show that this combination enables efficient navigation of combinatorial search spaces while handling highly constrained motions that exhibit a performance that is far superior to that of sampling-based approaches. We demonstrate our method on diverse benchmarks of increased complexities and compare the performance with state of the art algorithms for rotational assemblies (95.8% success vs. 70.8% prior work), interlocking puzzles (100% vs. 18%), large-scale formations up to 2,000 cubes (100% success where baselines timeout at 120 cubes), and 72 real-world CAD assemblies with 50+ parts (100% success). Importantly, our proposed method not only solves a much larger class of real complex assembly planning problems, but is also significantly faster (up to 7.4×) even for those cases that can be handled by state of the art algorithms. Our method requires only 1--3 physics simulator calls per part and operates without training data, generalizing across mechanical, consumer, and structural assemblies. This work establishes contact graph processing as a fundamental primitive for scalable assembly planning.

title: Rethink Repeatable Measures of Robot Performance with Statistical Query
abstract: A standardized robot-testing algorithm should satisfy accuracy, efficiency, and very importantly, repeatability—consistently yielding similar outcomes across multiple executions by different stakeholders. Achieving repeatability grows challenging with increasing complexity, intelligence, diversity, and inherent stochasticity in testing methods, robotic platforms, and environments. While existing efforts address repeatability through ethical, hardware, or procedural means, this study specifically targets algorithm-level repeatability, focusing on statistical query (SQ) algorithms commonly used in standardized evaluations. We propose a lightweight, adaptive modification for any SQ-based routine—including Monte Carlo, importance sampling, and adaptive sampling—guaranteeing provable repeatability with bounded accuracy and efficiency. Effectiveness is demonstrated across three cases: standardized manipulator testing, intelligent risk assessment for automated vehicles, and performance evaluation of humanoid robot locomotion.

title: Scheduling Robotic Cellular Manufacturing Systems with a Petri-Net-Based Monte Carlo Tree Search
abstract: This paper introduces PN-MCTS, a Petri-net-based Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) framework designed for scheduling robotic cellular manufacturing (RCM) systems. The approach integrates place-timed Petri nets (PNs) and MCTS to traverse the reachability graph of the PN, aiming to identify optimal or near-optimal sequences of transition firings. Key features of the method include a four-phase PN-based MCTS process, comprising selection, expansion, simulation, and backpropagation, along with an iterative deadlock pruning strategy and a deadlock penalty strategy, both of which enhance system robustness. In addition, a penalty decay mechanism is incorporated during backpropagation to reduce over-penalization of ancestral states, supporting a more balanced exploration of potential schedules. Experimental results show that PN-MCTS effectively alleviates the state-space explosion problem and achieves high-quality scheduling solutions with greater computational efficiency than PN-based A* search, while outperforming PN-based FIFO and SRPT dispatching rules in solution quality.

title: Intra-Rollout Self-Supervised Adaptation of Inverse Dynamics Models for Sub-Centimeter Precision Placement
abstract: Inverse dynamics models (IDMs) provide a compact interface for vision-based robotic manipulation, yet they frequently struggle with precision alignment tasks demanding sub-centimeter geometric tolerances. This limitation stems from the inherent spatial generalization gap between sparse offline demonstrations and the continuous real-world workspace, which causes residual spatial biases to persist under unseen deployment configurations. To bridge this gap, we propose intra-rollout self-supervised adaptation for IDMs, where model parameters are dynamically updated during task execution using transitions generated by the robot’s own actions. Because deterministic online execution often reinforces locally self-consistent, policy-induced errors, we introduce a bounded stochastic excitation mechanism with a decaying schedule to restore informative supervision while preserving closed-loop stability. We evaluate our approach on diverse real-world tabletop manipulation tasks, including coarse pick-and-place and a rigorous precision groove insertion benchmark requiring ≤ 0.5 cm spatial tolerance. Across both loose and tight tolerance regimes, intra-rollout adaptation substantially improves task success, enabling reliable sub-centimeter spatial alignment across novel configurations without the need for exhaustive data coverage, additional supervision, or force sensing.
presentations: Engineering Precision and Reliability in Automation

title: Hardware-Aware Scheduling Techniques and Model Reformulation for Real-Time AI Workloads on Heterogeneous Edge GPUs
abstract: Edge artificial intelligence (AI) devices, such as the NVIDIA Jetson series, integrate multiple accelerators, including CPUs, GPUs, and deep learning accelerators (DLAs), to efficiently execute deep neural network (DNN) workloads under strict power and latency constraints. Despite this hardware diversity, most deployed systems rely on GPU-only execution, leaving significant performance potential untapped. This paper analyzes practical scheduling strategies for heterogeneous NVIDIA Jetson devices and demonstrates that hardware-aware model reformulation expands the set of feasible accelerator mappings available to heterogeneous schedulers. Scheduling techniques developed for NVIDIA Jetson devices are studied, categorizing them by methodology (heuristic vs. optimization) and analyzing their treatment of key scheduling challenges: memory contention, transition costs, accelerator compatibility, and energy efficiency. Building on this review, we present a case study in which hardware-aware architectural refinement of a generative adversarial network (GAN)-based computed tomography (CT)-to-magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reconstruction model enables fully DLA-resident execution. Replacing DLA-incompatible deconvolution padding with cropping layers eliminates GPU fallback and expands the feasible scheduling design space. Under heterogeneity aware execution of concurrent deep neural networks (HaX-CoNN) multi-stream scheduling, the refined model achieves approximately 170 FPS for simultaneous MRI reconstruction and stroke detection, twice the performance of the original model, while maintaining structural similarity above 73%.

title: A Framework for Closed-Loop Robotic Assembly, Alignment and Self-Recovery of Precision Optical Systems
abstract: Robotic automation has transformed scientific workflows in domains such as chemistry and materials science, yet free-space optics, which is a high-precision domain, remains largely manual. Optical systems impose strict spatial and angular tolerances, and their performance is governed by tightly coupled physical parameters, making generalizable automation particularly challenging. In this work, we present a robotics framework for the autonomous construction, alignment, and maintenance of precision optical systems. Our approach integrates a hierarchical computer vision system, optimization routines, and custom-built tools to achieve this functionality. As a representative demonstration, we perform the fully autonomous construction of a tabletop laser cavity from randomly distributed components. The system performs several tasks such as laser beam centering, spatial alignment of multiple beams, resonator alignment, laser mode selection, and self-recovery from induced misalignment and disturbances. By achieving closed-loop autonomy for highly sensitive optical systems, this work establishes a foundation for autonomous optical experiments for applications across scientific domains.
keywords: Robotics and Automation in Life Sciences

title: Anytime Planning for End-Effector Trajectory Tracking
abstract: End-effector trajectory tracking algorithms find joint motions that drive robot manipulators to track reference trajectories. In practical scenarios, anytime algorithms are preferred for their ability to quickly generate initial motions and continuously refine them over time. In this paper, we present an algorithmic framework that adapts common graph-based trajectory tracking algorithms to be anytime and enhances their efficiency and effectiveness. Our key insight is to identify guide paths that approximately track the reference trajectory and strategically bias sampling toward the guide paths. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework by restructuring two existing graph-based trajectory tracking algorithms and evaluating the updated algorithms in three experiments.

title: Manageable Convex Region Iteration without Half-Plane Optimization for Robot Navigation in 2D Cluttered Scenes
abstract: To address the challenges of path safety and algorithm efficiency in robot navigation within complex environments, in this paper an integrated path optimization-following framework is proposed with a novel Manageable Convex Region Iteration without Half-Plane Optimization (MCRIwHPO). The path planning problem is modeled as a nonlinear optimization to generate a time-independent parameterized path. In MCRIwHPO, half-plane constraints via ellipse expansion (without additional optimization) are handled in the first stage , and the seed point inclusion constraint when calculating the maximum-area inscribed ellipse is handled in the second stage, ensuring convex region manageability. This two-stage design can gradually increase the ellipse area (the lower limit of the convex hull area) through iteration, thus enhancing the ability of the convex hull to approximate the free space. In path following, obstacle expansion reserves a safety threshold, and a preset performance controller limits following errors within this threshold to avoid collisions from external disturbances. The proposed MCRIwHPO is compared with existing algorithms in simulation scenarios with 5–20 obstacles. The results indicate that MCRIwHPO achieves the optimal convex region area with a stable computation time within 50 ms, meeting real-time requirements. This integrated optimization and following framework was also implemented in real-world scenarios using a four-wheel differential drive vehicle. The experimental results show that the vehicle avoids obstacles smoothly within a prescribed path following error and maintains stable velocity throughout the navigation process, further verifying the effectiveness and practical applicability of the framework.

title: Online Trajectory Optimization for Arbitrary-Shaped Mobile Robots Via Polynomial Separating Hypersurfaces
abstract: An emerging class of trajectory optimization methods enforces collision avoidance by jointly optimizing the robot's configuration and a separating hyperplane. However, as linear separators only apply to convex sets, these methods require convex approximations of both the robot and obstacles, which becomes an overly conservative assumption in cluttered and narrow environments. In this work, we unequivocally remove this limitation by introducing nonlinear separating hypersurfaces parameterized by polynomial functions. We first generalize the classical separating hyperplane theorem and prove that any two disjoint bounded closed sets in Euclidean space can be separated by a polynomial hypersurface, serving as the theoretical foundation for nonlinear separation of arbitrary geometries. Building on this result, we formulate a nonlinear programming (NLP) problem that jointly optimizes the robot's trajectory and the coefficients of the separating polynomials, enabling geometry-aware collision avoidance without conservative convex simplifications. The optimization remains efficiently solvable using standard NLP solvers. Simulation and real-world experiments with nonconvex robots demonstrate that our method achieves smooth, collision-free, and agile maneuvers in environments where convex-approximation baselines fail.

title: Safe Multimodal Replanning Via Projection-Based Trajectory Clustering in Crowded Environments
abstract: Fast replanning of the local trajectory is essential for autonomous robots to ensure safe navigation in crowded environments, as such environments require the robot to frequently update its trajectory due to unexpected and dynamic obstacles. In such settings, relying on the single trajectory optimization may not provide sufficient alternatives, making it harder to quickly switch to a safer trajectory and increasing the risk of collisions. While parallel trajectory optimization can address this limitation by considering multiple candidates, it depends heavily on well-defined initial guidance, which is difficult to obtain in complex environments. In this work, we propose a method for identifying the multimodality of the optimal trajectory distribution for safe navigation in crowded 3D environments without initial guidance. Our approach ensures safe trajectory generation by projecting sampled trajectories onto safe constraint sets and clustering them based on their potential to converge to the same locally optimal trajectory. This process naturally produces diverse trajectory options without requiring predefined initial guidance. Finally, for each trajectory cluster, we utilize the Model Predictive Path Integral framework to determine the optimal control input sequence, which corresponds to the local maxima of a multi-modal optimal trajectory distribution. We first validate our approach in simulations, achieving higher success rates than existing methods. Subsequent hardware experiments demonstrate that our fast local trajectory replanning strategy enables a drone to safely navigate crowded environments.

title: Primitive-Based Truncated Diffusion for Efficient Trajectory Generation of Differential Drive Mobile Manipulators
abstract: We present a learning-enhanced motion planner for differential drive mobile manipulators to improve efficiency, success rate, and optimality. For task representation encoder, we propose a keypoint sequence extraction module that maps boundary states to 3D space via differentiable forward kinematics. Point clouds and keypoints are encoded separately and fused with attention, enabling effective integration of environment and boundary states information. We also propose a primitive-based truncated diffusion model that samples from a biased distribution. Compared with vanilla diffusion model, this framework improves the efficiency and diversity of the solution. Denoised paths are refined by trajectory optimization to ensure dynamic feasibility and task-specific optimality. In cluttered 3D simulations, our method achieves higher success rate, improved trajectory diversity, and competitive runtime compared to vanilla diffusion and classical baselines. The source code is released at https://github.com/nmoma/nmoma .

title: Safe Planning in Unknown Environments Using Conformalized Semantic Maps
abstract: This paper addresses semantic planning problems in unknown environments under perceptual uncertainty. The environment contains multiple unknown semantically labeled regions or objects, and the robot must reach desired locations while maintaining class-dependent distances from them. We aim to compute robot paths that complete such semantic reach-avoid tasks with user-defined probability despite uncertain perception. Existing planning algorithms either ignore perceptual uncertainty—thus lacking correctness guarantees—or assume known sensor models and noise characteristics. In contrast, we present the first planner for semantic reach-avoid tasks that achieves user-specified mission completion rates without requiring any knowledge of sensor models or noise. This is enabled by quantifying uncertainty in semantic maps—constructed on-the -fly from perceptual measurements—using conformal prediction in a model- and distribution-free manner. We validate our approach and the theoretical mission completion rates through extensive experiments, showing that it consistently outperforms baselines in mission success rates.
keywords: Formal Methods in Robotics and Automation

title: SRMP: Search-Based Robot Motion Planning Library
abstract: Motion planning is a critical component in any robotic system. Over the years, powerful tools like the Open Motion Planning Library (OMPL) have been developed, offering numerous motion planning algorithms. However, existing frameworks often struggle to deliver the level of predictability and repeatability demanded by high-stakes applications -- ranging from ensuring safety in industrial environments to the creation of high-quality motion datasets for robot learning. Complementing existing tools, we introduce SRMP (Search-based Robot Motion Planning), a new software framework tailored for robotic manipulation. SRMP distinguishes itself by generating consistent and reliable trajectories, and is the first software tool to offer motion planning algorithms for multi-robot manipulation tasks. SRMP easily integrates with major simulators, including MuJoCo, Sapien, Genesis, and PyBullet via a Python and C++ API. SRMP includes a dedicated MoveIt! plugin that enables immediate deployment on robot hardware and seamless integration with existing pipelines. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate in this paper that SRMP not only meets the rigorous demands of industrial and safety-critical applications but also sets a new standard for consistency in motion planning across diverse robotic systems. Visit this https://srmp.readthedocs.io/ for SRMP documentation and tutorials.
keywords: Path Planning for Multiple Mobile Robots or Agents

title: UCON: Uncertainty-Aware Navigation with Historical Re-Association in Dynamic Environments
abstract: Autonomous navigation in dynamic environments is hindered by two fundamental challenges: perception instability and uncertainty–optimization mismatch. The former leads to identity switches and unreliable motion estimation, while the latter prevents principled incorporation of motion uncertainty into trajectory optimization. To address these challenges, we propose UCON, an uncertainty-aware navigation algorithm in dynamic environments. For perception instability, we present a point-level historical re-association mechanism that leverages historical point cloud fragments to recover lost targets while maintaining identity continuity. Subsequently, a Kalman filter is employed to provide anisotropic motion state estimation and covariance propagation. To resolve the uncertainty–optimization mismatch, we transform predicted states and their covariances into uncertainty sectors, which are embedded as differentiable cost terms within a trajectory optimization framework. This achieves consistent uncertainty-aware dynamic obstacle avoidance while maintaining smoothness and feasibility. Extensive simulations and real-world experiments demonstrate that, while maintaining high computational efficiency, UCON achieves superior perception stability and robust navigation performance in dynamic environments compared to state-of-the-art methods. The code will be open-sourced to facilitate further research.

title: Collision Avoidance from Monocular Vision Trained with Novel View Synthesis
abstract: We consider the task of reactive collision avoidance during locomotion in a known indoor scene. Our proposal is a two-stage visuomotor pipeline trained entirely from Gaussian-splatting synthetic data that operates on monocular RGB images. First, we train a visual encoder on photorealistic images rendered by 2D Gaussian splatting, using monocular depth estimation as a proxy task to obtain a latent space that captures scene geometry. Second, we train a policy correcting user-commanded velocities by reinforcement learning over the resulting latent space. The full pipeline trains in a few hours on a single GPU. At inference, only the encoder and the lightweight policy run onboard, bypassing the need for a depth sensor or explicit scene reconstruction. We evaluate our method on a wheeled-biped robot with limited onboard compute and compare it against a range-sensing baseline, showing that the approach applies fewer velocity corrections and performs better even under scene variations.

title: NeHMO: Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability Learning for Decentralized Safe Multi-Arm Motion Planning
abstract: Safe multi-arm motion planning is a challenging problem in robotics due to its high dimensionality, coupled configuration space, and complex collision constraints. Centralized planners are capable of coordinating all arms but often face scalability limitations, restricting applicability in realtime settings. On the other hand, decentralized methods are scalable and recent deep learning-based approaches have shown promising results. However, these depend on accurate behavior prediction or coordination protocols and may fail when other arms act unpredictably. To address these challenges, we introduce a neural Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability (HJR) learningbased approach to approximate a safety value function that captures worst-case inter-arm safety constraints. We further develop a decentralized trajectory optimization framework that uses the learned HJR representation for real-time planning. The proposed method is scalable and data-efficient, generalizes across multi-manipulator systems, and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on challenging multi-arm motion planning tasks.

title: OGM-CBF: Occupancy Grid Map-Based Control Barrier Function for Safe Mobile Robot Control with Memory of Out of View Obstacles
abstract: Safe control in unknown environments is a key challenge in mobile robotics. Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) provide a principled framework for guaranteeing safety constraint satisfaction. State-of-the-art CBF approaches assume either known environments with predefined obstacles, or rely only on obstacles currently within the robot’s Field of View (FoV). However, practical robots in a priori unknown environments can observe their surroundings only partially, and therefore can violate safety due to limited FoV, sensor range, or occlusion. This paper incorporates the memory of previously observed obstacles of arbitrary shape that have left the robot's FoV into CBF-based safe control. In particular, we couple the Signed Distance Function (SDF)-based CBF formulation to an occupancy grid map built online during the system's operation. Furthermore, the lack of steering authority induced by the SDF gradient degeneracy when facing obstacles head-on is addressed by constructing a Gaussian pyramid of the SDF, yielding a multi-level CBF. The efficacy of the proposed approach is evaluated against memory unaware baselines in the CARLA simulator. Moreover, we demonstrate the generalizability of the proposed approach in real deployments on a small warehouse robot and a large, articulated frame steering autonomous wheel loader.

title: D-SafeMPC: Diffusion-Driven Safe Model Predictive Control with Discrete-Time Control Barrier Functions
abstract: A key limitation on the use of diffusion models in robotic planning is their inability to inherently enforce safety or dynamical constraints, which often results in physically infeasible or unsafe outputs. Hybrid approaches that employ model predictive control (MPC) to address this problem can be unstable, as poor trajectory initializations from the diffusion model prevent the MPC from converging to a safe and feasible solution. To overcome these challenges, we propose D-SafeMPC, which enhances the interaction between diffusion and control. Our method guides the reverse diffusion process with control barrier functions (CBFs) and control Lyapunov functions (CLFs) and employs an iterative-projection scheme where an MPC refines the trajectory at each denoising step. This steers sampling toward safe, goal-directed regions and provides reliable MPC warm starts. In simulations on a Franka manipulator across four scenarios (one static-obstacle and three dynamic-obstacle settings) and in a sim-to-real experiment on a physical Franka robot, D-SafeMPC improves safety, task success rates, and planning efficiency over state-of-the-art baselines. To facilitate reproducibility, our source code and experimental configurations are available in a repository at https://github.com/erdiphd/D-SafeMPC

title: SAGE-CBF: A Scalar-Aware Graph Equivariant Control Barrier Function Framework for Decentralized Safe Multi-Agent Navigation
abstract: Ensuring robust safety and scalability is a critical challenge for decentralized large-scale Multi-Agent Systems (MAS). Existing learning-based Control Barrier Function (CBF) methods often underutilize the geometric structure of MAS, limiting scalability, geometric generalization, and sample-efficient learning. While frame-canonicalized methods improves generalization, they can introduce unstable local reference frame and suppress the directional asymmetry needed to resolve symmetric stagnations. To overcome these challenges, we propose SAGE-CBF (Scalar-Aware Graph Equivariant CBF), a novel framework that integrates geometric equivariance with explicit reflection-symmetry breaking. By processing intrinsic invariant scalars and goal-anchored chiral pseudo-scalars, our approach restricts the local symmetry group from O(2) to SO(2), preserving the asymmetry needed to resolve symmetric interactions. We further introduce a terminal basis synthesis architecture that guarantees strict SE(2) equivariance and provides structural alignment with the gradient directions induced by the scalar CBF features. Extensive empirical results demonstrate that SAGE-CBF successfully generalizing to 512-agent deployments, maintaining an over 90% success rate, and outperforms representative data-driven and canonicalized equivariant baselines in high-density navigation and symmetric deadlock resolution.

title: PolyMerge: Compressing 3D Gaussian Splats with Polytope Coverings for Provably Safe Resource-Constrained Navigation
abstract: Obstacle avoidance is essential for safe navigation and motion planning. Recent advances in radiance field reconstruction have enabled object detection and modeling with unprecedented fidelity, but remain too memory- and compute-intensive for deployment in on-board robotic perception and motion planning. To address these limitations, we propose PolyMerge to transform a large, photorealistic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model of a scene into a lightweight representation as a set of convex polytopes whose enclosed volume is guaranteed to over-approximate all obstacles in the original 3DGS model. PolyMerge uses a variable number of polytopes to trade off conservativeness and computational cost, and integrates with polytope-based control barrier functions (CBFs) to ensure collision-free path planning. We showcase PolyMerge in simulation and hardware experiments using a small Crazyflie drone, which uses PolyMerge to compute and follow safe trajectories in real time using extremely limited onboard compute resources, outperforming baselines in speed while guaranteeing safety.

title: Design of a Biomimetic Joint-Covering Skin with Tissue-Like Structure to Enhance Proprioception in a Musculoskeletal Humanoid
abstract: Proprioception in musculoskeletal humanoids is typically estimated primarily from muscle sensing, while the role of cutaneous deformation around joints remains insufficiently explored. In biological systems, mechanoreceptors distributed within soft tissue complement muscle feedback and support reliable joint state estimation. This study presents the design of a biomimetic joint-covering skin with a tissue-like layered structure that integrates pressure- and stretch-sensitive elements within the joint-covering tissue. The proposed skin is implemented on the musculoskeletal humanoid Musashi-W, and its independent proprioceptive capability as well as its integration with muscle sensing are evaluated. Experimental results show that the proposed skin alone achieves joint angle estimation with an average error of approximately 3 degrees. Furthermore, integration with muscle sensing improves estimation accuracy. Owing to its joint-covering structure, the skin may mechanically mitigate the influence of external disturbances on the muscles, and the integration of multiple modalities suggests the possibility of contributing to the identification of external stimuli that are difficult to interpret using muscle sensing alone. This work presents a design methodology for biomimetic joint-covering skin and demonstrates that such tissue-structured skin can serve as an effective approach for extending proprioceptive systems in musculoskeletal humanoids through multimodal sensing.

title: Online Class-Aware Bayesian Terrain Parameter Estimation for Off-Road Vehicles
abstract: Terrain classification using exteroceptive sensors is a common component of off-road navigation systems, with basic approaches assigning each class a predefined traversability cost. In order to provide more accurate terrain characterization, this paper proposes online estimation of terrain-vehicle interaction parameters for each terrain class using Bayesian filters. A novel method for estimating the magnitude of terrain-induced vibrations is combined with filters for estimating either the slip ratio or understeer gradient, depending on vehicle type. The ability of the method to characterize terrain is validated on four different data sets and three different vehicles. Furthermore, it is shown that the method for vibration estimation has similar performance to a previous artificial neural network-based end-to-end approach, while being more explainable. To study filter performance on Nordic terrain, we present the Swedish off-road (SWORD) dataset for proprioceptive terrain characterization, which contains data for ten different terrain classes, including multiple types of snow and ice. The dataset is available online at https://github.com/swedish-off-road-dataset.

title: Proprioceptive Safe Active Navigation and Exploration for Planetary Environments
abstract: Deformable granular terrains introduce significant locomotion and immobilization risks in planetary exploration and are difficult to detect via remote sensing such as vision. Legged robots can sense terrain properties through leg–terrain interactions during locomotion, offering a direct means to assess traversability in deformable environments. However, how to systematically exploit this interaction-derived information for navigation planning remains underexplored. We address this gap by presenting PSANE, a Proprioceptive Safe Active Navigation and Exploration framework that leverages leg–terrain interaction measurements for safe navigation and exploration in unknown deformable environments. PSANE learns a traversability model using Gaussian Process regression to estimate and certify safe regions and identify exploration frontiers online, and integrates these estimates with a reactive controller for real-time navigation. Frontier selection is formulated as a multi-objective optimization problem that balances safe-set expansion probability and goal-directed cost, with subgoals selected through scalarization over the Pareto-optimal frontier set. PSANE safely explores unknown granular terrain and reaches specified goals using only proprioceptively estimated traversability, while achieving performance improvements over baseline methods.

title: Unified Static–Dynamic Macro–Micro Robotic Palpation with Multi-Actuation for Viscoelastic Property Mapping
abstract: Robotic palpation offers a more repeatable, quantitative touch-based assessment beyond subjective human examination. However, robotic palpation remains constrained by a fundamental tradeoff between large-workspace exploration and high-bandwidth contact interaction. We overcome this limitation by combining industrial robotic positioning with localized voice-coil actuation for multi-actuation macro--micro robotic palpation. A robot arm provides global surface coverage, while a directly mounted voice coil actuator (VCA) enables high-resolution quasi-static indentation and dynamic frequency sweep excitation with synchronized force and displacement sensing. We model this framework, linking indentation-derived stiffness to frequency-domain system identification and enabling decomposition of effective mass, stiffness, and damping during contact. We verify this model through one-dimensional phantom experiments, seeing a clear measured stiffness difference between solid, hollow and rigid insert samples. We further demonstrate the power of this approach by conducting two-dimensional phantom experiments on a soft surface with embedded air channels. We demonstrate a robust linear relationship between internal channel pressure and applied probing force (R^2 ≈ 0.99). These results establish that our hybrid VCA-robot arm method provides spatial stiffness measurements that reliably resolve subsurface features.

title: Keeping It Smooth: The Role of Haptic Feedback in Shaping Motor Performance
abstract: Training for complex motor tasks, such as those encountered in minimally invasive surgery, benefits from effective performance feedback mechanisms to accelerate skill acquisition and ensure retention. Prior work has demonstrated that haptic feedback based on movement smoothness quantified by the metric spectral arc length (SPARC), when provided in real-time as trainees perform complex motor tasks, can cause beneficial changes in task completion strategies resulting in faster completion times without loss of accuracy. The concept of movement smoothness is abstract, however, and more intuitive measures of movement smoothness like idle time and average velocity can be good alternatives to SPARC. Here, we demonstrate the effect of real-time objective performance feedback of movement smoothness, conveyed through a vibrotactile cue encoding alternative measures of movement smoothness, compared to feedback based on SPARC. Subjects receiving smoothness-based feedback based on average velocity performed the task fastest, but their accuracy was lower than the other two groups. We evaluated the effect of removing feedback for additional trials, and showed that performance improvements ceased. After training, the three groups were indistinguishable from each other.
